rejected.title: Visual illusions
card: A visual illusion is a case where what a person sees does not match what is really there. It shows that perception is the brain's interpretation of the input from the eyes, and the interpretation can be wrong.
Müller-Lyer illusion
two lines of equal length look unequal because of the arrowheads at their ends. The line with outward-pointing fins looks longer than the line with inward-pointing fins.
Ames room
a specially built room that looks like an ordinary square room from one viewing point. Two people of similar height standing in its far corners look very different in size.
Agnosia
a person sees an object clearly but cannot recognise it. Their eyes work, but the brain does not link what is seen to its meaning.
rejected.remember: Illusions show that vision can be wrong. In agnosia, the person sees the object but cannot recognise it.

a.q: What does the Müller-Lyer illusion show about visual perception?
opts: The brain misreads accurate input from the eyes
The eyes send a faulty image of the lines to the brain
The fins change the real length of the two lines
Perception is an exact copy of what the eyes take in
a.why: The two lines are equal, and the eyes take them in normally, yet they look unequal. The error comes from how the brain interprets the arrowheads. It is not a faulty image from the eyes, and the fins do not change the lines' real length.
a.clue: The lines are equal, so where does the error come from?

b.q: After a stroke, Tomas can describe the shape and colour of a toothbrush in his hand but cannot say what it is for. His eyesight tests as normal. What is the best explanation?
opts: Agnosia, as he sees the toothbrush but cannot recognise it
A visual illusion, as the toothbrush looks a different size
Blindness, as his eyes cannot send the image to the brain
An Ames room effect, as the toothbrush looks distorted
b.why: Tomas sees the toothbrush, since he can describe its shape and colour, but cannot recognise it. This is agnosia. An illusion is a misperception of what is there, and he is not misjudging the toothbrush's size or shape.
b.clue: Can he see the object? Can he tell what it is?
